title: Abraham
summary: The patriarch called from Ur to follow God into promise, faith, and covenant formation.
historical_context: Abraham stands in the ancestral narratives of Genesis as the father of the covenant line. His story reflects clan migration, land promise, and divine promise in an early biblical setting rather than a fixed modern chronology.
ancient_near_east_context: The narrative world includes household religion, kinship loyalty, land inheritance, and covenant-making patterns familiar across the ancient Near East.
literary_context: Genesis uses Abraham as the hinge between primeval history and the story of Israel. Later biblical writers return to him as an interpretive anchor for faith, promise, and inclusion of the nations.
covenantal_significance: Abraham embodies the initial covenant promises that later unfold through Israel, David, and the new covenant in Christ.
interpretive_notes: Do not flatten Abraham into a mere moral example; Genesis presents him first as a recipient of promise.
Later Jewish, Christian, and Pauline readings all appeal to Abraham, but they emphasize different facets of the same covenant story.
common_questions: What promises did God make to Abraham?
How does Abraham shape later biblical theology?

scripture_references.notes: Paul draws Abraham into the gospel argument
